title: Summer Refinement Series, Part 3: Refining Cold Call as a Cognitive Support
author: SoL in the Wild
summary: The author of SoL in the Wild, a classroom teacher, shares the third installment of her Summer Refinement Series—focused on how she plans to rethink Cold Call as a cognitive support rather than merely a participation technique. The article situates Cold Call within a broader cognitive science framework: routines that become predictable and psychologically safe allow students to direct cognitive resources toward thinking rather than social risk management. Drawing on Rosenshine's Principles of Instruction, the author argues that Cold Call done well serves as a retrieval practice mechanism, a checking-for-understanding tool, and a metacognitive prompt that keeps all students mentally engaged. She distinguishes between Cold Call as accountability theater—where students perform alertness—and Cold Call as genuine cognitive support that scaffolds active thinking and distributed practice across a full class period.
points: Cold Call is most powerful when it functions as retrieval practice: randomly selecting students to answer after independent think time activates memory processes and signals that all students need to hold information in working memory.
The routine must be psychologically safe before it becomes cognitively useful: if students experience Cold Call as a gotcha moment, anxiety consumes working memory that should be devoted to thinking.

Rosenshine's Principles support Cold Call as a checking-for-understanding tool: high rates of checking student understanding—through Cold Call and other routines—correlate strongly with student achievement gains.
Cold Call distributes cognitive engagement across the whole class, not just volunteers: when only willing students answer, the others can coast; Cold Call changes the cognitive contract for everyone.
Successful implementation requires explicit instruction in how Cold Call works: students need to understand the purpose—active thinking—so they see it as a support rather than a test of preparedness.
quotes: These refinements emerged from reflecting on my practice and thinking about how evidence from cognitive science and the science of learning can better inform my curriculum and explicit instruction.
In previous posts, I explored how I am making my Africa unit, and ultimately all of my units, more knowledge-rich through improved curriculum sequencing and coherence.
Cold Call, done well, keeps every student in the room cognitively accountable. Done poorly, it becomes a performance of alertness that has nothing to do with actual learning.
Rosenshine's research showed that effective teachers ask a large number of questions and check the responses of all students. Cold Call is the structural tool that makes this possible at scale.
The goal is not to catch students who aren't paying attention. The goal is to create a classroom where not paying attention is cognitively difficult—because thinking is the default.
